chunks: Ibn Nuh said: Abu Nasr Hibatullah ibn Bint Umm Kulthum bint Abi Ja'far al-Amari informed me, saying: Abi Ja'far Muhammad ibn Uthman al-Amari had compiled books on jurisprudence, which he had heard from Abu Muhammad al-Hasan (peace be upon him), and from the Companion (peace be upon him), and from his father Uthman ibn Sa'id, from Abu Muhammad and from his father Ali ibn Muhammad (peace be upon them). Among them were books titled: The Books of Drinks. Al-Kabira, Umm Kulthum bint Abi Ja'far (may Allah be pleased with her), mentioned that these books reached Abul-Qasim al-Husayn ibn Ruh (may Allah be pleased with him) at the time of the bequest to him, and remained in his possession. Abu Nasr said: I suspect she said that they reached Abul-Hasan al-Samuri (may Allah be pleased with him and be pleased with him) afterwards.

key_terms.السَّمُرِيِّ: Al-Samuri (Abul-Hasan Muhammad ibn Umar al-Samuri, a key figure in the Minor Occultation)
key_terms.الصَّاحِبِ: The Companion (referring to Uthman ibn Sa'id al-Kummi)

ai.seo_question: Who possessed the jurisprudential books of Muhammad ibn Uthman al-Amari during the occultation?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Kitab al-Ghayba* underscores the continuity of scholarly authority during the Minor Occultation by tracing the custody of Muhammad ibn Uthman al-Amari’s jurisprudential works, particularly the *Books of Drinks*, through the four prominent Deputies. It highlights the tangible transmission of hadith literature from the Imams to the scholarly class, reinforcing the legitimacy of the Deputies as custodians of religious knowledge. The specific mention of the *Books of Drinks* reflects the detailed legal scrutiny applied to social practices like wine consumption, a key theme in early Shia fiqh.
